chunks:
Since 2020, both Australia and New Zealand used very large, coordinated fiscal and monetary stimulus to cushion COVID‑19, then shifted to tighter monetary policy and more restrained fiscal settings to tackle inflation—but New Zealand’s response was proportionally larger, its monetary tightening earlier and more aggressive, and its later cost‑of‑living support more tightly targeted than Australia’s.[1][2][3][4][5][6][7][8]

## Starting points in 2019–early 2020

Australia entered the pandemic with low government debt, below‑target inflation and growth slightly below potential, supported by a long‑standing inflation‑targeting framework and flexible exchange rate.  New Zealand also had low public debt and strong macro institutions, which Treasury and international observers later highlighted as enabling a “go hard, go early” response.[5][9][10]

## COVID‑era fiscal policy: scale and design

Australia’s federal and state fiscal response totalled roughly 9–10% of GDP, with Commonwealth spending alone estimated at about 7–8% of GDP and state/territory measures around 2%.  Key measures included the JobKeeper wage subsidy, JobSeeker and other income supplements, tax incentives for investment, and schemes such as HomeBuilder and SME Recovery Loan to support housing and small business.[2][1]

New Zealand structured its economic response around a “three waves” framework—fight the virus and cushion the blow, kick‑start recovery, and reset/rebuild—with fiscal policy at the centre.  It created a COVID‑19 Response and Recovery Fund (CRRF) that ultimately reached NZD 61.6 billion, with NZD 58.4 billion allocated—about 22% of 2019 GDP once combined with the initial NZD 12.1 billion response package—covering wage subsidies, business grants, health spending, and social support.[7][5]

## COVID‑era fiscal instruments: wage subsidies and targeted transfers

Australia’s JobKeeper program provided a flat wage subsidy to employers to keep workers attached to their jobs, complemented by direct household support such as Economic Support Payments and a Coronavirus Supplement on JobSeeker.  These measures helped limit job losses and supported incomes, contributing to a relatively rapid rebound in GDP and employment by early 2021.[1][2]

New Zealand’s Wage Subsidy Scheme supported approximately 1.6 million jobs in its first phase, with eligibility tied to revenue losses and refined over time, alongside income support measures such as benefit increases, a temporary COVID Income Relief Payment, and winter energy payment enhancements.  Additional programs like Resurgence Support Payments and Jobs for Nature grants targeted firms during lockdowns and supported regional employment and environmental projects.[10][5]

## COVID‑era monetary policy: ultra‑loose and unconventional

The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) cut the cash rate twice in March 2020 to 0.25%, then to 0.1% in November 2020, and introduced unconventional tools such as three‑year government bond yield targeting, a term funding facility for banks, and later a bond‑purchase program.  These measures aimed to reduce funding costs, support credit to households and businesses, boost asset prices (including housing), and put downward pressure on the Australian dollar.[1]

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) cut the Official Cash Rate (OCR) from 1.0% to 0.25% in March 2020 and signalled it would remain there for at least a year, while launching a Large‑Scale Asset Purchase (LSAP) program that initially envisaged buying up to NZD 60 billion of government bonds.  RBNZ also removed loan‑to‑value ratio restrictions, delayed planned bank capital increases, and supported mortgage deferrals to keep credit flowing and soften the downturn.[11][12][10]

## Pandemic outcomes and recovery phase

Australia’s GDP fell by about 7% in the June 2020 quarter, its largest contraction since the Second World War, and unemployment peaked around 7.5% in August 2020, but by March 2021 GDP had surpassed its pre‑pandemic level as fiscal and monetary stimulus, reopening and tax incentives lifted consumption and investment.  IMF assessments note that Australia’s post‑pandemic recovery remained stronger than peers, supported by private and public investment and strong net exports, even as high inflation and tighter financial conditions later weighed on household consumption.[13][2][1]

New Zealand’s GDP fell sharply in early 2020 but only about 2% on an annual basis, with unemployment peaking around 5.2% from a pre‑COVID 4.1%, outcomes that official reviews attributed partly to the speed and generosity of the fiscal and monetary response.  By 2021–22, high vaccination rates and a shift to a “living with COVID” strategy, alongside gradual border reopening, allowed the economy to recover while policy priorities moved from emergency support to longer‑term resilience and wellbeing.[14][5]

## Transition to tightening: inflation and monetary policy

Both countries faced a surge in inflation from 2021–22 as global supply shocks, strong domestic demand and housing pressures took hold, but New Zealand started tightening earlier and more aggressively.  OECD and RBNZ sources highlight that RBNZ began raising the OCR from late 2021, delivering significant rate hikes through 2022–23 to bring inflation—which peaked around 7.2%—back into its 1–3% target range.[3][6][8]

Australia’s inflation rose above the RBA’s 2–3% target band, with headline CPI reaching mid‑single digits in 2022, prompting the RBA to shift from ultra‑loose settings to a series of cash‑rate increases and an unwinding of QE.  By late 2024 headline inflation had fallen to roughly 2.4%, within the target band, but core inflation and services prices remained higher, indicating more persistent domestic pressures than in New Zealand.[4][2][13]

## Fiscal stance post‑2022: consolidation and cost‑of‑living

Australia gradually wound down pandemic programs like JobKeeper and targeted new spending towards infrastructure and defence, but faced criticism for not doing enough to offset cost‑of‑living pressures as real household disposable incomes fell sharply relative to other OECD countries.  OECD‑based analysis shows that Australian households saw an 8% decline in real per‑capita disposable income in the two years to March 2024, the sharpest drop in the OECD, reinforcing political focus on cost‑of‑living rather than broad new stimulus.[2][4]

New Zealand closed the CRRF in Budget 2022, repurposing its remaining NZD 3.2 billion to health contingencies, offsetting other spending, and a NZD 1 billion package to help low‑ and middle‑income households manage rising living costs.  The 2022 Budget introduced a one‑off NZD 350 “cost of living payment” for individuals earning under NZD 70,000 (outside the existing winter energy support), extended temporary cuts to fuel excise and half‑price public transport, and made permanent 50% public transport discounts for Community Services Card holders, while keeping the overall fiscal stance contractionary from 2023 onward.[6][7]

## Debt and fiscal sustainability

Australia’s pandemic‑era deficits lifted government debt from around the mid‑40s percent of GDP in 2019 to over 57% in 2020, but subsequent growth and partial consolidation stabilized debt near the low‑50s percent range by the mid‑2020s.  IMF and OECD reports stress maintaining prudent fiscal policy while addressing structural issues like slowing productivity, high household debt and housing affordability.[9][15][4]

New Zealand’s large, temporary fiscal expansion was explicitly framed as time‑limited, and the government’s projections and external commentary indicated a return to surplus by fiscal year 2024/25, with net debt remaining moderate by advanced‑economy standards.  Treasury documents underline a shift from COVID‑specific envelopes to integrating response and resilience spending into normal budget processes, while keeping debt on a sustainable path.[16][17][6][7]

## Comparative table: key economic policy choices since 2020

| Policy area | Australia | New Zealand |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Overall COVID fiscal scale | Commonwealth plus states around 9–10% of GDP, with Commonwealth stimulus estimated at 7–8% of GDP. [2] | Combined initial package and CRRF allocations around NZD 70+ billion, roughly 22% of 2019 GDP. [5][7] |
| Fiscal architecture | Standard budget process with emergency packages and industry‑specific schemes (JobKeeper, HomeBuilder, SME loans). [1][2] | Dedicated COVID‑19 Response and Recovery Fund (CRRF) plus “three waves” strategy guiding allocations across health, business and social supports. [7][5] |
| Wage subsidies and income support | JobKeeper wage subsidies, JobSeeker supplements, one‑off support payments, tax incentives and early superannuation access. [1][2] | Wage Subsidy Scheme, Resurgence Support Payments, benefit increases, targeted cash transfers like COVID Income Relief Payment and enhanced winter energy support. [10][5] |
| Initial monetary easing | Cash rate cut to 0.25%, then 0.1, introduction of yield‑curve control, term funding facility and QE bond purchases. [1] | OCR cut to 0.25%, forward guidance to hold for at least a year, LSAP QE programme, relaxation of LVR rules and bank capital timelines. [11][10] |
| Timing/intensity of tightening | Tightening from 2022 in response to above‑target inflation, with multiple rate hikes and withdrawal of unconventional measures; inflation back within 2–3% band by late 2024 but core pressures persistent. [2][13][4] | OCR increases from late 2021 through 2023; OECD and RBNZ note “significant” tightening that effectively reined in inflation from about 7.2% to within 1–3% target range; OCR later cut to 3.25% from August 2024. [3][8][6] |
| Cost‑of‑living policy response | Focus on broad tax and transfer system plus some energy rebates, but OECD data show the sharpest fall in real household disposable incomes in the OECD, sparking political debate about adequacy of support. [4] | Targeted cost‑of‑living package (NZD 350 payments for lower‑income individuals, extended fuel excise and transport subsidies, permanent discounts for low‑income public transport users) designed to be temporary and fiscally contained. [6][7] |
| Post‑COVID fiscal stance | Gradual consolidation with ongoing infrastructure and defence investment; emphasis on maintaining prudence while addressing structural issues. [13][15] | CRRF closed; budget documents project return to surplus around 2024/25, with overall government spending expected to be contractionary from 2023 onwards. [6][7][17] |

## Key similarities and differences

Both countries relied on large wage subsidies, income support and unprecedented monetary easing to prevent mass unemployment and business failures, and both achieved relatively fast GDP recoveries compared with initial pessimistic scenarios.  However, New Zealand’s total fiscal envelope was much larger relative to GDP, its monetary tightening started earlier and was more forceful, and it used a more explicitly time‑limited, ring‑fenced fiscal architecture than Australia.[8][3][5][7][10][13][14][2][1]

In contrast, Australia’s stimulus was somewhat smaller in relative terms and its later cost‑of‑living response has been criticized in light of the sharp decline in real household incomes, even though headline inflation has returned to target.  New Zealand combined aggressive early tightening with narrowly targeted cost‑of‑living measures and a quicker pivot to fiscal consolidation, accepting higher interest rates in the short term but aiming to protect lower‑income households while keeping debt and inflation under control.[3][4][6][7][8][2]

sources.name: Australia: 2021 Article IV Consultation-Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Australia
sources.snippet: 1. Australia entered the pandemic with sound macroeconomic fundamentals but growth below potential. Mining investment had stabilized following years of adjustment after the mining boom, and housing prices had just started rising following the 2017–19 decline. The economy was supported by sound macroeconomic management, including prudent fiscal policy, an inflation targeting framework, and exchange rate flexibility. However, growth remained below potential, and inflation undershot the Reserve Bank of Australia’s (RBA) target range. Despite generally strong fundamentals with low government debt and a well-capitalized banking sector, some structural vulnerabilities remained. These included slowing labor productivity growth, high household debt, and elevated banking sector loan concentration in residential mortgages.

sources.name: Economic Recovery Plan for Australia - Overview
Australia: 2023 Article IV Consultation-Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Australia
sources.snippet: 1. Australia’s post-pandemic recovery remained stronger than peers’, even as high inflation and tighter financial conditions are weighing on household consumption. The slowdown in households’ consumption growth was, however, offset by resilient private investment supported by public investment in transport, health, education, and national defense. Net exports contributed to growth on the back of robust sales of coal and service exports buoyed by inflows of foreign students, migrants, and tourists. As a result, the job market remained tight and inflation more persistent than envisioned. The sizable, positive output gap in 2023 is projected to narrow in the near term. More persistent inflation, de-anchoring of inflation expectations, and external-demand shocks are among the visible risks to the near-term.

entities.description: Since 2020, both Australia and New Zealand implemented unprecedented fiscal and monetary stimulus measures to counter the profound economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Australia's post-pandemic recovery was supported by resilient private investment and public spending, which helped the economy remain stronger than many peers despite facing high inflation and tighter financial conditions.
New Zealand has focused on tightening monetary policy since late 2021, which has proven effective in curbing inflation as part of its post-pandemic economic management.

New Zealand's pandemic response relied on central government borrowing and reprioritizing spending to fund wage subsidies, public health measures like contact tracing, and business recovery initiatives to support its "go hard, go early" health strategy.
To manage its financial response, New Zealand utilized the COVID-19 Response and Recovery Fund (CRRF) from 2020 to 2022 as a flexible fiscal management tool rather than a fixed sum of money.
New Zealand’s monetary policy shifted from easing to tightening between 2021 and 2023 by raising interest rates to counter high inflation and work toward its 1–3% inflation target.
